column121: On a flight from ZZZ to ZZZ1; I was flying north over Location X at 4000MSL about 25NM east of ZZZ2; I experienced a partial engine failure and forced landing; likely due to fuel starvation or lack of fuel pressure.  While flying I initially noticed that my right tank was about 1/4 tank and my left was 3/4+ full.  This is a normal flight characteristic in my aircraft.  The right tank always burns faster than the left until it gets down to 1/4 and then the left starts to catch up.  About 10 min later; during my fuel scan; I could not see a line on the right side or the left side.  This was not normal; so I started to climb to about 6000MSL. In my assessment the best course of action was to continue flying down Location X; because there was an airstrip about 10-12 miles downriver. Any other option was much farther.  During the climb I rocked the wings and could see that my right tank was almost empty; and the left tank was completely full.  About 4 minutes later my engine started to lose power.  It never completely lost power. The propeller continued to turn; but it wasn't making enough power to maintain altitude. Based on the Garmin/engine data after the fact the engine was still barely running but only making about 10% power.At this point I started descending into Location X. I scanned for any possible place to land but didn't find anything. After turning a bend in the river; I spotted a small bench above the river; so I committed to landing there. It didn't appear that I would make it to ZZZ3. I performed a poweroff 180 and landed in approx 300ft facing south.  After landing; my aircraft scraped some small trees and brush; causing some minor damage.  Mostly cosmetic; since it is a fabric aircraft. After inspecting the aircraft damage and cause of the failure I discovered that the left fuel tank fuel cap was not completely seated.  This caused a vacuum in the fuel tank which prevented the fuel from the left tank from flowing into the header tank. Once on the ground the full tank cross fed fuel to right tank.  At this point I had 2 half tanks of fuel on each side. Approximately 2 hours' worth of fuel.After a thorough inspection and several runups of the aircraft over 2 days with remote assistance from the manufacturer; previous owner; and several others; I was able to make some minor repairs to damaged fabric areas using duct tape.  I was able to successfully fly the aircraft to ZZZ2; approx 20 min to the west. then ultimately to ZZZ4 where I made the repairs and the aircraft was then inspected and returned to service.

column121: The incident occurred during a training flight after take off. I took control from the student at an altitude of 300ft AGL then executed the 'impossible 180 turn' and landed back on the runway. The student pilot was a candidate for a private pilot certificate. At the time he had almost 20-25 hours of flight time. The lesson objective was to teach normal take off and landings and pattern work at a non-towered airport. The aircraft rotation speed is 67kts; and initial climb at 72kts. At 400 AGL; 600 MSL we would clean up by retracting flaps to the up position; and reduce the power load from a 100% to below 92% and climb at 88kt for cruise climb. When retracting the flaps to the up position; it sinks. When power is reduced to 92%; a change of engine pitch (noise) can be easily noticed. At 300ft AGL; 500ft MSL; that change of pitch (noise) occurred. My first thought was that the student initiated an early clean up procedure. I asked and he responded 'I am not sure what is happening' I took control; reduced pitch; and reduced power; then I added power up to see if anything changes but the engine was not advancing any farther than 40%.I am very familiar with the area and my only options departing North from runway XX was a street which is covered by trees or back to the runway. straight ahead was a warehouse; to the left is a quarry and trees; to the right is a gas station. I initiated a right turn from the beginning so it was going to be the Street or back to the airport; at the moment I noticed a little grass field behind the airport hangers so I aimed for that and made my first ratio call 'ZZZ traffic; Aircraft X engine failure returning to the runway; stay clear' in that time; the power lever was at full power with 40% load given. I reduced the power level to idle and back again to full with the same results of 40% which wouldn't let the aircraft climb but to hold altitude. When I realized that I was not losing altitude; I decided to cross the hangars and land on the ramp or taxi way; and then I decided that I had enough altitude and energy to land on  the runway. I made another radio call 'ZZZ traffic; Aircraft X engine failure returning to the runway stay clear'. I conducted a safe landing and was able to clear the runway. We came to a full stop and taxied off the runway to the taxi way. and turned off the plane. I checked on my student which he was fine and honestly very calm though out the whole process. I called my chief pilot and explained everything that happened. We also did some trouble shooting on the taxi way which wasn't successful. Me and the student taxied the plane to the ramp. We also contacted the aircraft owner and our maintenance team. In an hour we had the mechanic; the chief pilot; the aircraft owner all at the airport to diagnose the problem. It was found that the shaft mechanism that opens and closes the waste gate for the turbo to spin is connected to the waste gate by a pin that had snapped off during take off. Which closed shut the waste gate and didn't allow exhaust gas to spin the turbines for the turbo. As a result; the ECUs put the aircraft on what is known as a 'Limp mode' to reduce further damage and protect the engine. After the problem was addressed. I and the mechanic conducted a couple of high power sittings on the ground; a couple of run up; a rejected take off; and a lap in the pattern. Everything checked out and I flew the plane back to ZZZ1 which is about a 30 min flight. There was a service bulletin for that exact issue by Diamond Aircraft Industries. I believe that would have prevented this incident. I also believe a better understanding of the 'Limp Mode' would have made me make a quicker decision.Overall; it was a great teaching moment for everyone involved. and thank god for everyone's safety.
